n: Abijah died and his son Asa became king. Asa’s reign began with ten years of peace — in Chronicles, a sign of God’s blessing on faithfulness.

f.w: the land was quiet ten years

n: Asa did what was good and right in God’s eyes — the Chronicler’s highest praise for a king.
He removed foreign altars and hill shrines, smashed sacred pillars, and cut down Asherah poles — cleaning out the idolatry that had crept in under earlier kings.

f.g: Standing stone pillars used in Canaanite worship.
Hebrew asherim — wooden poles or images honoring the goddess Asherah.

n: Reform was not only removing evil but commanding good: Asa called Judah to seek the Lord and keep His law.

f.g: A key phrase in Chronicles: to turn to God in worship, prayer, and obedience.

n: He removed the high places and incense altars from every city, and the kingdom enjoyed peace under him.
Asa used the years of peace to fortify cities. God gave rest, and Asa used rest wisely to prepare.

f.w: the LORD had given him rest

n: Asa told Judah to build while the land was still theirs, testifying that their peace came from seeking God. Prosperity is a time to prepare, not to relax.

f.w: while the land is yet before us
f.g: While the land is still open to us and under our control.

f.w: we have sought him, and he hath given us rest

n: Asa’s army was large: 300,000 from Judah with large shields and spears, and 280,000 Benjamite archers with small shields.
Zerah the Cushite invaded with a massive army of “a thousand thousand” — a way of saying an overwhelming host — and 300 chariots, reaching Mareshah in Judah’s foothills.

f.g: A Cushite commander, possibly serving Egypt or ruling Cushite settlers in the south; his exact identity is debated.
A million — likely a round figure meaning a vast, countless army.

n: Asa went out to meet him and set up battle lines in the Zephathah valley near Mareshah.
Asa’s prayer is a classic of faith: Lord, it makes no difference to You whether those You help are strong or weak. We rely on You and go in Your name; don’t let mere man win against You.

f.w: it is nothing with thee to help

n: The Lord struck the Cushite army before Asa and Judah, and they fled. The battle is credited to God.
Judah chased them to Gerar in the southwest. The invaders were crushed “before the LORD, and before his host,” and Judah took a great deal of plunder.

f.g: A town in the western Negev, near Gaza.
God’s army — Judah fighting as the Lord’s troops.

n: Judah also defeated the towns around Gerar, which were terrified by the Lord, and took much plunder from them.

f.w: the fear of the LORD came upon them

n: They attacked the herdsmen’s camps, took many sheep and camels, and returned to Jerusalem. Some of this spoil was offered to the Lord in the next chapter.
